who: Environmental and technology historian, formerly University of Virginia; PhD in biology, Michigan, 1993.

evidence.says: Russell's CV lists Michigan's biology PhD (1993), Virginia appointments from 1994 to 2012, and dissertation co-supervision of Thomas Finger, Jaime Allison and Eric Stoykovich. Allison's and Stoykovich's dissertation titles match the supplied records.

Identifies Edmund P. Russell as a historian working in environmental history and history of technology, with LC identifier n00010744 and appointments at Kansas, Boston University and Carnegie Mellon, matching the CV.

notes: Direct student matches establish identity. The CV gives Finger's completion as 2015 rather than the supplied 2014 and calls Allison Jaime rather than James.

who: Alan S. Christy, historian of Japan at UC Santa Cruz; PhD, University of Chicago.

evidence.says: Lists Alan S. Christy as a history professor studying early modern and modern Japan, with a Chicago PhD and publications including Rethinking Japanese History.
Christy's autobiographical university page says he joined UCSC's History Department in 1995 and has spent his entire career there.
The authority identifies Alan S. Christy through Rethinking Japanese History and a 2011 UCSC faculty page describing him as an associate professor and East Asian studies director.

notes: Authority, institution, field and doctoral university agree. The faculty page does not specify the PhD year.

who: Richard T. Farrell, American historian at the University of Maryland, College Park.

evidence.says: A 1979 Indiana Magazine of History review is signed Richard T. Farrell, University of Maryland, College Park.
The Richard T. Farrell authority is based on Richardson on Evidence (1985), a legal work.
Brooklyn Law School's notice identifies its professor Richard Farrell as the author of Prince, Richardson on Evidence and a faculty member since 1964.
Another Richard Farrell authority identifies an author at Boeing Aerospace Company through Integrated Cuing Requirements Study (1983).

notes: The same-name law authority n88640352 belongs to a different academic. Other supplied authorities concern different names or works; none was positively connected to the Maryland historian. The limited evidence does not exclude every remaining candidate.

who: David LaVerne Gross, modern European intellectual historian at Colorado Boulder; PhD in history, Wisconsin-Madison.

evidence.says: The authority identifies David LaVerne Gross and associates him with The Writer and Society (1979).
The obituary for David Laverne Gross records a Wisconsin-Madison history PhD and employment teaching history at Colorado Boulder from 1969 to 2018.
The publisher-supplied biography for Lost Time describes David Gross as professor of modern European intellectual history at Colorado Boulder and author of The Past in Ruins.

notes: Full name, degree institution, field and employment period agree. The separate David L. Gross authority n82052423 concerns Pleistocene stratigraphy.

who: Erich E. Haberer, historian at Wilfrid Laurier University; PhD, University of Toronto.

Laurier's 2018-19 graduate calendar lists Erich Haberer as an associate professor of history with a Toronto PhD.
The Erich E. (Erich Edmund) Haberer authority cites Laurier's 2011 website identifying Erich Haberer as associate professor and author of Jews and Revolution in Nineteenth-Century Russia.

notes: Direct dissertation-supervisor evidence and the authority's Laurier affiliation establish the match.

who: Max Krochmal, historian of modern U.S. civil rights and labor, formerly TCU; history PhD, Duke, 2011.

The authority identifies the author of Blue Texas through TCU's 2016 faculty page, noting Duke studies and work on modern U.S., African American and labor history.
His institutional biography confirms the Duke PhD (2011), authorship of Blue Texas and previous employment as a history professor at TCU.

who: Rebecca Nedostup, historian of modern China at Brown; history PhD, Columbia, 2001.

Brown lists Rebecca A. Nedostup as associate professor of history and East Asian studies and identifies her first book as Superstitious Regimes.
The authority identifies Rebecca Nedostup as the author of Superstitious Regimes (2009) and then an assistant professor of history at Boston College.

notes: The CV connects the authority's earlier Boston College affiliation to Brown during the supplied students' period; doctorate and book also agree.

who: John J. Reardon, historian at Loyola University Chicago and author of studies of Edmund and Peyton Randolph.

evidence.says: The authority identifies John Joseph Reardon through Peyton Randolph (1982); its citation to America and the Multinational Corporation (1991) describes him as professor of history at Loyola University.
The publisher identifies John J. Reardon as professor of history at Loyola University in Chicago and author of Edmund Randolph: A Biography (1974) and Peyton Randolph (1982).
The other John J. Reardon authority is based on This Grace Filled Moment (1984), rather than the Loyola historian's works.

notes: The candidate authority explicitly places him in Loyola history in 1991, matching the students' institution and period. The supplied Georgetown doctorate was not independently verified.
